subtopic: Talking to someone lying or hiding
passage:
Come here, Arnab, you look worried about the results. Sit. I'm Joseph, and I have been where you are. At sixteen I failed my whole year and I hid it. I took the report card out of the letterbox before anyone saw it and told my parents "results next month." I dreaded every dinner.
For six weeks I was alone with it. I stopped talking to my friends and felt sick each time the phone rang. Hiding felt safer for a day, then heavier every day.
In the end my older sister found the crumpled card and just sat with me. I cried for an hour. My parents were sad, but they helped me plan the repeat year. I wish I had told them sooner.

qa.q: How long was Joseph alone with the secret?
qa.a: Joseph was alone with it for six weeks.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling during the weeks of hiding the report card?
qa.a: Joseph felt afraid and lonely, dreading every dinner and feeling sick when the phone rang. Hiding seemed safer at first but grew heavier.

qa.q: What turning point helped Joseph, and what followed?
qa.a: Joseph's older sister found the crumpled card and sat with Joseph, who cried for an hour. The parents were sad but helped plan the repeat year.

qa.q: How might Joseph's older sister have felt finding the card?
qa.a: Joseph's sister was probably worried and gentle, choosing to sit beside Joseph without scolding. Being calm made it safe to cry and tell the truth.

grounding: A teenager conceals a failed year, expecting disapproval, and finds concealment increases isolation and fear, told by an elder.

passage:
The house was full of pre-exam noise, and Kavitha, sixteen, moved her rice around the plate. She and Saurabh, her closest friend since Class 6, had stopped speaking two weeks ago after a quarrel about a borrowed notebook. Now their whole group of friends had gone quiet around her.
"Everything okay at school?" her mother asked.
"Fine," Kavitha said. Her stomach hurt. She was sure her mother would say it was her own fault.
She ate in her room, told herself she did not care, and lay awake anyway. Just before midnight she knocked on her mother's door and said, "Amma, can I tell you something? It isn't going well with Saurabh."

qa.q: Since which class had Kavitha and Saurabh been friends?
qa.a: They had been friends since Class 6.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling when she said "Fine" with her stomach hurting?
qa.a: Kavitha was afraid of being blamed and felt lonely. Saying "Fine" hid it, but her hurting stomach and pushed-around rice show how she was carrying it.

qa.q: What did Kavitha do at midnight that changed things?
qa.a: Kavitha knocked on her mother's door and said it was not going well with Saurabh. Telling someone she trusted ended the hiding.

qa.q: How might Kavitha's mother have felt when Kavitha said "Fine"?
qa.a: Kavitha's mother probably sensed something was wrong but did not push, and was likely relieved when Kavitha came to her. Asking a simple question left the door open.

grounding: A teenager conceals trouble with a friend, expecting blame, and finds hiding increases isolation and fear until she speaks up.

subtopic: Talking to someone lying or hiding
passage:
In the school hostel, the Class 11 results were posted on the board on Friday. Dhruv had failed physics and would have to repeat the year.
On the phone that night, his mother asked, "Results?" He said, "Not out yet." On Sunday he said it again.
He stopped going to the common room, where everyone was talking about Class 12 subjects. He ate at odd hours to avoid his roommate, Omkar. At night he lay awake, heart racing, imagining his father's face.
Omkar finally caught him at the washbasins. "Dhruv, I saw the board. I'm not going to tell anyone. But you look awful."
Dhruv's eyes stung. "I haven't told my parents. I keep lying."
"Do you want to call them with me here? Or tell the warden first?"
Dhruv thought. "The warden. Then my parents. Today."
They walked to the warden's office together.

qa.q: Which subject did Dhruv fail?
qa.a: Dhruv failed physics.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv keep saying the results weren't out?
qa.a: Dhruv felt ashamed and afraid of his father's disappointment, so hiding the result felt safer in the moment.

qa.q: What helped Dhruv move from hiding to telling?
qa.a: Omkar noticed without judging, promised privacy and offered to be there, which made telling the warden and his parents feel possible.

qa.q: How did hiding the result affect Dhruv's life in the hostel?
qa.a: Hiding made Dhruv lonely and more anxious, avoiding the common room and his roommate and lying awake at night.

grounding: A teenager hides a failed year expecting disapproval, and concealment increases isolation and fear until he tells.

subtopic: Talking to someone lying or hiding
passage:
Dear Gargi,

I'm writing this because I can't say it on the phone. I have to repeat Class 10.

I found out in May. I didn't tell you. I didn't tell anyone except my parents. When you asked about results, I said I was "waiting for the rechecking". There was no rechecking.

I thought if I told you, you'd think I was stupid, or you'd find new friends who were moving ahead. So I stopped replying to the group. I stopped going to Rukhsana's birthday. I told everyone I had fever.

Hiding it felt safe for a week. Then it just felt lonely. Every message from you made my stomach hurt, because I'd have to lie again.

So here it is. I'm repeating the year. I'm not stupid; I was sick during the exams and fell behind.

Will you still write to me?

Salma

qa.q: What did Salma tell Gargi when asked about results?
qa.a: Salma claimed to be "waiting for the rechecking".

qa.q: What was Salma afraid would happen if Gargi knew?
qa.a: Salma was afraid Gargi would think Salma was stupid and would find new friends who were moving ahead.

qa.q: What could Gargi do to help Salma after reading the letter?
qa.a: Gargi could write back warmly, say the friendship is unchanged, and invite Salma back into the group so Salma feels less alone.

qa.q: What was hiding the truth like for Salma after the first week?
qa.a: Hiding felt lonely and painful for Salma, with every message making Salma's stomach hurt because another lie would be needed.

grounding: A teenager conceals repeating a school year, expecting disapproval, and hiding increases loneliness and fear.

subtopic: Talking to someone lying or hiding
passage:
So, people ask me what the hardest part of Class 12 was, and I always say: not the exams. It was hiding a crush for a whole year. I'm Devika, by the way.
His name was Ujjwal. He sat two rows ahead in chemistry and drew little rockets in the margins. That's it. That's all it was. But my family is strict about these things, and my cousins would have teased me for months, and I was sure my mother would think I'd stop studying.
So I hid it. From everyone. I stopped going to the canteen in case my face gave it away. I deleted a message I'd typed to my best friend four times. I sat alone with this huge, silly feeling and no one to laugh about it with.
The funny thing? When I finally told my best friend, after the exams, she laughed and hugged me and said, "I knew! Why didn't you tell me?" A year of hiding, and she'd have kept it safe.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal draw in the margins?
qa.a: Ujjwal drew little rockets in the margins.

qa.q: Why did Devika hide the crush from everyone?
qa.a: Devika was afraid of the strict family's disapproval and the cousins' teasing, and worried that Mother would expect studying to stop.

qa.q: What could have made that year easier for Devika?
qa.a: Trusting one safe person, like the best friend, earlier, so Devika wouldn't have carried the feeling alone.

qa.q: How did Devika's best friend react to finally hearing the truth?
qa.a: The best friend felt amused and warm, laughing and hugging Devika, and a little hurt that Devika hadn't told her sooner.

grounding: A teenager hides a crush expecting disapproval, and concealment feels safe but brings isolation.

subtopic: Talking to someone lying or hiding
passage:
Monday: Deepak's maths result came back, 23 out of 80. He folded the sheet into his geometry box and told Mummy the papers weren't checked yet. It felt like a door clicking safely shut.
Thursday: a parents' meeting notice for next week. Deepak didn't hand it over. He skipped cricket, sat alone in the library pretending to revise, and snapped at Sangeeta didi when she asked why he was so quiet. At night he lay awake rehearsing what he'd say when they found out.
The next Tuesday: Sangeeta found him on the terrace. "You haven't laughed in a week. What's going on?" Deepak's throat closed. Then he pulled out the folded sheet. She read it, sat beside him and said, "Okay. That's bad, not the end. Let's tell Mummy together before the meeting." For the first time in eight days, Deepak's shoulders dropped.

qa.q: What did Deepak score in maths?
qa.a: 23 out of 80.

qa.q: How was Deepak feeling by Thursday?
qa.a: Deepak felt anxious and isolated, skipping cricket, snapping at his sister and lying awake afraid of being found out.

qa.q: What could Deepak try the next time something goes wrong at school?
qa.a: Tell one trusted person early, like Sangeeta didi, before hiding turns a bad mark into a week of fear and loneliness.

qa.q: What was it like for Sangeeta watching Deepak that week?
qa.a: Sangeeta noticed he had not laughed in a week and was worried, and got snapped at when she asked, until he finally showed her the sheet.

grounding: Shows a teenager hiding a failed maths result out of shame, feeling safe at first but growing more isolated and afraid until he tells his sister.
